{
  "analyses": [
    {
      "paper_id": "2606.13814",
      "title": "TASR: Training-Free Adaptive Stopping for Iterative Retrieval",
      "research_question": "Can iterative RAG stop adaptively without a learned stopping controller by combining answer stability with calibrated model confidence while preserving answer quality and reducing retrieval calls?",
      "methodology": "TASR evaluates an iterative RAG loop in which one additional passage from a fixed pre-ranked list is revealed per round, up to five rounds. Its stopping predicate fires when the normalized answer is unchanged from the previous round and a per-round isotonic calibration of the first answer-token logit margin exceeds 0.25; the calibrator is fitted on a 100-question tune split but no classifier, value head, or trajectory-trained policy is learned. The rule was selected from an exhaustive enumeration of 381 candidate stopping rules and evaluated across distractor, open-domain BM25, dense-retrieval, multiple-model, and large-model configurations using F1, LLM-call count, and paired bootstrap confidence intervals.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "Across the primary three-model by two-dataset distractor grid, TASR reached 57.40 macro F1 at 3.13 calls, compared with 53.98 F1 at 3.00 calls for fixed-k=3, while retaining 94.8% of fixed-k=5 F1 with 62.6% of its calls.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.1 Headline"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Three primary cells showed statistically significant F1 improvements over fixed-k=3 and the remaining three were statistical ties, with no significant regression in the primary grid.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.2 Per-Cell Breakdown"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The fixed stopping rule transferred to open-domain BM25, dense retrieval, and a Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B scale stress test without significant regressions in the reported extension experiments.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.6-5.8 External Validity, Retriever Robustness, and Scale Robustness"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Verbalized confidence was highly collapsed on the studied RLHF-tuned models, while first-answer-token logit margins provided much stronger separation between correct and incorrect answers.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.4 Negative Results on Alternative Signals and 5.9 Cross-Model Analysis"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The margin threshold protects against some premature stops caused by an answer becoming stable before the required evidence has entered the context.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "3.4 The TASR Predicate"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Among the 381 enumerated candidate rules used in rule selection, the chosen answer-stability plus calibrated-margin rule was not Pareto-dominated by an alternative under the paper's search procedure.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.3 The Exhaustive Search Behind AS_m25"
        }
      ],
      "limitations": [
        "The stopping signal depends on access to token log probabilities and a structured short-answer generation format, which limits direct transfer to APIs that hide logits or to substantially different response formats.",
        "Each per-round isotonic calibrator is estimated from only 100 tuning examples, so calibration reliability under larger distribution changes is uncertain.",
        "The experiments primarily concern short-answer factoid and multi-hop QA; long-form generation, semantic answer equivalence, and claim-level evidence completeness are not validated.",
        "Retrieval is from a fixed pre-ranked list with no query reformulation, so the method does not decide what evidence should be fetched next.",
        "The method reports LLM-call count as its principal cost measure rather than measured end-to-end latency or monetary cost.",
        "The rule provides an empirical quality-cost tradeoff but no formal bounded-risk or anytime-valid stopping guarantee.",
        "Temporal validity, document-version provenance, and permission-aware access control are outside the evaluated controller state."
      ],
      "reproducibility": {
        "code_available": true,
        "dataset_available": true,
        "metrics_reported": true
      },
      "confidence_scores": {
        "primary_quality_cost_gain": 0.99,
        "no_significant_primary_regressions": 0.99,
        "cross_retriever_and_scale_transfer": 0.96,
        "logit_margin_beats_verbalized_confidence": 0.99,
        "margin_reduces_premature_stopping": 0.97,
        "enumerated_rule_pareto_result": 0.97
      },
      "raw_claims": [
        "TASR stops only after the current normalized answer matches the previous answer and calibrated margin exceeds the fixed threshold.",
        "The only fitted TASR component is a per-round one-dimensional isotonic calibrator rather than a learned stopping policy.",
        "The primary evaluation uses HotpotQA and 2WikiMultiHopQA distractor settings with separate tuning and evaluation questions.",
        "The rule cannot stop after the first retrieval round because answer stability requires two consecutive answers.",
        "TASR improves macro F1 over the fixed three-round baseline at nearly the same average number of calls in the primary grid.",
        "No primary evaluation cell shows a statistically significant regression relative to fixed-k=3.",
        "Open-domain and dense-retrieval extensions reuse the locked stopping design rather than retuning a new stopping policy for each cell.",
        "Verbalized confidence often saturates at its maximum value and is less discriminative than the answer-token logit margin.",
        "Pure answer stability can stop on a repeated wrong answer before useful evidence arrives.",
        "The experiments leave query reformulation and coarser retrieval-step granularity for future work."
      ],
      "source_url": "https://arxiv.org/html/2606.13814",
      "access": "full_text"
    },
    {
      "paper_id": "2510.14337",
      "title": "Stop-RAG: Value-Based Retrieval Control for Iterative RAG",
      "research_question": "Can a learned value function over iterative RAG trajectories determine whether the expected benefit of another retrieval step justifies continuing rather than stopping?",
      "methodology": "Stop-RAG casts iterative RAG as a finite-horizon Markov decision process with STOP and CONTINUE actions and constructs an offline training set from every prefix of fully executed retrieval trajectories. For each state, the authors estimate stopping rewards using eight independent answer generations scored by F1 and train a DeBERTa-v3-large value network with full-width forward-view Q(lambda) targets for both actions. At inference time, the controller compares estimated STOP and CONTINUE values and applies a validation-tuned stopping threshold. Evaluation covers MuSiQue, HotpotQA, and 2WikiMultihopQA in both the authors' RAG pipeline and a CoRAG integration.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "Within the authors' own iterative RAG pipeline, Stop-RAG improves EM, F1, and reported accuracy over both the unmodified fixed-iteration pipeline and LLM-prompted stopping on all three evaluated benchmarks.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "6.1 Main Results"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The abstract-level statement that Stop-RAG consistently outperforms both baselines across benchmark settings is contradicted by the CoRAG HotpotQA result, where Stop-RAG is slightly below the unmodified CoRAG baseline and does not dominate LLM-Stop.",
          "evidence_type": "contradicted",
          "section": "6.1 Main Results"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Stop-RAG is portable enough to be attached to a separately developed CoRAG pipeline, where it improves MuSiQue and 2WikiMultihopQA results despite the HotpotQA exception.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "6.1 Main Results"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The learned controller generally retains more useful retrieval evidence than prompting-based LLM stopping, although it can use slightly more retrieval steps than the prompted stopper.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "6.2 Analysis: Retrieval Results"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The full-width forward-view Q(lambda) objective performs better on the reported MuSiQue ablation than binary classification, Monte Carlo targets, and the Q(0) variant.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "6.2 Analysis: Ablation Study"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Training is offline: complete trajectories are collected first, every prefix becomes a candidate state, and no online environment interaction is required while fitting the controller.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "4 Stop-RAG"
        }
      ],
      "limitations": [
        "The learned controller requires pipeline-specific trajectory generation and supervised value-function training rather than being training-free.",
        "Generating training targets is computationally expensive because complete retrieval trajectories are executed and stopping rewards are estimated with eight answer-generation trials per state.",
        "Evaluation is restricted to three multi-hop QA datasets and two RAG pipeline configurations.",
        "The CoRAG HotpotQA result demonstrates that plug-and-play transfer does not guarantee an improvement in every pipeline-dataset combination.",
        "The stopping threshold is selected on validation data.",
        "The controller state used in the implementation does not explicitly model structured evidence gaps, document versions, temporal validity, or permissions.",
        "The objective predicts downstream answer value but does not provide a calibrated statistical bound on the risk of stopping incorrectly."
      ],
      "reproducibility": {
        "code_available": true,
        "dataset_available": true,
        "metrics_reported": true
      },
      "confidence_scores": {
        "own_pipeline_consistent_gain": 0.99,
        "abstract_consistency_claim_has_exception": 0.99,
        "cross_pipeline_portability": 0.96,
        "retrieval_quality_tradeoff": 0.94,
        "q_lambda_ablation_advantage": 0.98,
        "offline_training": 0.99
      },
      "raw_claims": [
        "Stop-RAG models each retrieval decision as a choice between stopping and continuing in a finite-horizon MDP.",
        "Its offline dataset includes every nonterminal prefix of complete iterative RAG trajectories.",
        "Stopping reward estimates use multiple answer generations from a state and F1 against the gold answer.",
        "The experiments use eight answer-generation trials when estimating state rewards.",
        "The value model learns estimates for both STOP and CONTINUE actions using Q(lambda) targets.",
        "The evaluation uses MuSiQue, HotpotQA, and 2WikiMultihopQA.",
        "Stop-RAG improves all three datasets in the authors' own pipeline.",
        "On CoRAG with HotpotQA, Stop-RAG does not outperform the original CoRAG configuration.",
        "The method is designed as a separate controller and does not require modifying the generator model itself.",
        "The reported ablation favors the Q(lambda) training formulation over the tested alternative objectives."
      ],
      "source_url": "https://arxiv.org/html/2510.14337",
      "access": "full_text"
    },
    {
      "paper_id": "2406.10490",
      "title": "Active, anytime-valid risk controlling prediction sets",
      "research_question": "Can risk-controlling prediction sets be extended to sequential and actively labeled data so that risk control remains valid at every stopping time while labels are acquired efficiently under a budget?",
      "methodology": "The paper builds anytime-valid risk-controlling prediction sets using betting-based e-processes, yielding a time-uniform guarantee over the entire sequential process rather than a guarantee only at a predetermined sample size. It extends the construction to adaptive label acquisition through randomized labeling policies and inverse-propensity correction, and adds a learned conditional-risk predictor as a variance-reduction control variate. The authors analytically characterize optimal predictors and label-allocation policies under a labeling budget and derive regret results relating estimation error to e-process growth. Numerical simulations and ImageNet experiments compare label-all, oblivious random sampling, pretrained, and online-learned active policies.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "The paper establishes an anytime-valid risk-control guarantee that holds simultaneously over all time steps, allowing the procedure to be stopped adaptively without invalidating the stated risk guarantee under its assumptions.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "2 Anytime-Valid Risk-Controlling Prediction Sets"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Adaptive label sampling with inverse-propensity correction preserves the validity of the e-process construction while allowing the expected labeling rate to be constrained by a budget.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "3 Active Anytime-Valid Risk Control"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The theoretically optimal auxiliary predictor is the conditional expected risk given the features, and the optimal labeling probability is related to the conditional residual variability under the budget constraint.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "3 Active Anytime-Valid Risk Control"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Prediction error and deviation of the learned sampling policy from the optimal policy reduce expected wealth growth and therefore statistical efficiency, with this loss characterized by the paper's regret analysis.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Theorem 3 and Section 5.3"
        },
        {
          "finding": "In both the numerical simulations and ImageNet experiments, the pretrained and learned active policies reach better prediction-set utility for a given number of queried labels than the label-all and oblivious strategies while the observed safety-violation rate remains below the configured level.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "4 Experiments"
        }
      ],
      "limitations": [
        "The central theoretical development primarily assumes i.i.d. data, and the authors explicitly identify test-time distribution shift as an unresolved extension.",
        "The theory uses a lower-bounded labeling policy and an existence assumption for the analytically optimal sampling policy.",
        "Empirical validation is limited to simulations and ImageNet rather than retrieval, language generation, or evidence-adjudication systems.",
        "The method controls a mathematically specified prediction risk; it does not itself define how free-form evidence completeness or omission risk should be measured.",
        "The framework does not model temporal document versions, source provenance, or permission-aware retrieval.",
        "Applying the guarantees to adaptive RAG would require defining an appropriate bounded loss and justifying how retrieval-induced non-i.i.d. dependence fits the statistical assumptions."
      ],
      "reproducibility": {
        "code_available": true,
        "dataset_available": true,
        "metrics_reported": true
      },
      "confidence_scores": {
        "anytime_valid_risk_control": 0.99,
        "active_sampling_preserves_validity": 0.99,
        "optimal_predictor_and_sampling_characterization": 0.98,
        "regret_links_estimation_to_efficiency": 0.97,
        "empirical_label_efficiency": 0.96
      },
      "raw_claims": [
        "The proposed RCPS guarantee is time-uniform rather than valid only at one fixed sample size.",
        "The construction uses nonnegative betting e-processes and Ville-type maximal inequalities.",
        "Labels may be queried adaptively according to probabilities that depend on the observed feature vector.",
        "Inverse-propensity weighting corrects for selective label acquisition.",
        "An auxiliary prediction of conditional risk is used to reduce variance without being required for validity.",
        "The optimal auxiliary predictor equals the conditional expectation of the risk given the observed features.",
        "The optimal sampling rule allocates more labeling probability where residual risk variability is larger, subject to the budget.",
        "The empirical study compares active policies with labeling every example and with oblivious random labeling.",
        "Pretrained and learned policies are more label-efficient in the reported simulation and ImageNet studies.",
        "The authors identify distribution shift as a major direction not covered by the primary i.i.d. analysis."
      ],
      "source_url": "https://arxiv.org/html/2406.10490",
      "access": "full_text"
    },
    {
      "paper_id": "2609.16301",
      "title": "CLEAR: Cross-Source Evidence Adjudication for Large Language Models in Medicine",
      "research_question": "Can an LLM improve medical reasoning by keeping parametric, curated-local, and dynamically retrieved evidence separate, explicitly adjudicating disagreements among them, and selectively performing additional retrieval when existing evidence remains unresolved?",
      "methodology": "CLEAR independently produces candidate answers from parametric knowledge, a locally curated corpus, and dynamically retrieved evidence, retaining source-specific evidence and provenance for each pathway. An aggregation verifier examines the candidates together with evidence, provenance, and source-quality signals such as authority, recency, and content type, after which override-guard and challenge-audit mechanisms decide whether to preserve or revise the current conclusion. Unresolved disagreement can trigger a targeted, bounded follow-up query followed by re-adjudication rather than unrestricted search. The framework is evaluated with o3-mini and Qwen-3.5-9B across ten public medical benchmarks, with ablations for evidence-source combinations and follow-up retrieval.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "CLEAR shows its largest gains when the backbone's parametric baseline is weaker; for Qwen-3.5-9B, the best reported CLEAR configurations substantially improve MedQA and NEJM-QA over direct inference and conventional retrieval baselines.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "3.1 Results on MCQ Datasets and 4.1 Main Findings"
        },
        {
          "finding": "For o3-mini across MedQA, PubMedQA, and NEJM-QA, the full three-source CLEAR configuration has the highest aggregate score even though the best individual method varies by dataset.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "3.3 Ablation Studies"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Targeted follow-up retrieval on Qwen-3.5-9B increases aggregate performance from 77.22 to 78.13, while only 12 of 123 triggered follow-up searches produce an accepted answer revision.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "3.3 Ablation Studies"
        },
        {
          "finding": "External retrieval is not uniformly beneficial: when the o3-mini parametric baseline is already strong, additional evidence can provide little benefit and the default CLEAR configuration degrades performance on HealthBench.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "4.1 Main Findings"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The architecture preserves the identity and provenance of parametric, local, and dynamic evidence until adjudication, making cross-source agreement and conflict explicit instead of merging all retrieved context before reasoning.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "2 Methods"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The dynamic-evidence override guard requires relevance, credible sourcing, explicit support, and an explanation of why the competing conclusion is less appropriate before dynamic evidence is allowed to overturn stronger existing conclusions.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "2 Methods: Override Guard"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The framework's source-quality assessment explicitly permits recency to influence evaluation of dynamically retrieved evidence, providing a mechanism for time-sensitive evidence adjudication.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "2 Methods: Dynamic-Evidence Pathway"
        }
      ],
      "limitations": [
        "All evaluations are offline benchmark studies and do not establish clinical effectiveness, patient safety, or readiness for deployment.",
        "Public medical benchmarks may overlap with model pretraining or post-training data, and the authors cannot fully rule out parametric memorization.",
        "Dynamic web evidence can vary over time, complicating provenance stability and exact reproducibility.",
        "Institutional access restrictions, privacy requirements, and data governance are identified as deployment issues but are not implemented or empirically evaluated as permission-aware controller constraints.",
        "The adjudication logic is substantially prompt- and rule-driven and may itself be sensitive to model post-training behavior.",
        "Broader validation is needed across backbone families, retrievers, search systems, and application domains.",
        "The framework tracks source provenance and recency but does not present a formal version model for mutable documents or a statistical bounded-risk guarantee for stopping follow-up retrieval.",
        "The verifier's confidence output is an operational judgment rather than a demonstrated calibrated probability of correctness."
      ],
      "reproducibility": {
        "code_available": true,
        "dataset_available": true,
        "metrics_reported": true
      },
      "confidence_scores": {
        "larger_gain_with_weaker_parametric_backbone": 0.99,
        "cross_source_aggregate_advantage": 0.97,
        "targeted_followup_gain_and_selectivity": 0.99,
        "retrieval_not_uniformly_beneficial": 0.99,
        "provenance_preserving_adjudication": 0.99,
        "override_guard_constraints": 0.99,
        "recency_aware_source_quality": 0.98
      },
      "raw_claims": [
        "CLEAR keeps parametric, local-corpus, and dynamic-search candidates as separate evidence pathways before aggregation.",
        "Each pathway carries provenance information into the aggregation stage.",
        "Dynamic source quality can depend on authority, recency, and content type.",
        "The aggregation verifier explicitly reasons about agreement and disagreement among source-specific candidates.",
        "A dynamic source is not automatically allowed to override agreement from other pathways merely because it is newer.",
        "Unresolved conflicts can generate a targeted follow-up query and another adjudication round.",
        "Follow-up retrieval is used selectively rather than as an unconditional extra search step.",
        "The reported benefits are larger for the weaker Qwen backbone than for the stronger o3-mini baseline in several tasks.",
        "On some strong-backbone settings, retrieval provides little benefit or lowers performance.",
        "The evaluation uses public multiple-choice and free-text medical benchmarks rather than private patient records.",
        "The paper explicitly identifies changing search results and external-source reproducibility as deployment concerns."
      ],
      "source_url": "https://arxiv.org/html/2609.16301",
      "access": "full_text"
    },
    {
      "paper_id": "2605.03534",
      "title": "SURE-RAG: Sufficiency and Uncertainty-Aware Evidence Verification for Selective Retrieval-Augmented Generation",
      "research_question": "Can a structured set-level verifier determine whether retrieved evidence is sufficient to support a candidate answer and use uncertainty-aware selective prediction to abstain when that support is inadequate?",
      "methodology": "SURE-RAG uses a shared DeBERTa-v3-base cross-encoder to produce support, refutation, and neutral relation distributions for claim-evidence pairs, then aggregates those local outputs into answer-level coverage, relation-strength, uncertainty, and retrieval feature blocks. A logistic-regression aggregator predicts Supported, Refuted, or Insufficient, and an uncertainty-penalized selective score determines whether the system answers or abstains; calibration parameters and thresholds are selected only from development data. The main HotpotQA-RAG v3 benchmark contains 4,026 examples in 900 question groups with full, partial, hard-insufficient, irrelevant, and refuting evidence conditions and group-disjoint splits. Evaluation includes classification F1, selective risk at fixed coverage, calibration error, shortcut diagnostics, counterfactual evidence swaps, a GPT-4o audit, no-oracle variants, HaluBench transfer, and ablations.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "On controlled HotpotQA-RAG v3, calibrated SURE-RAG reaches 0.9075 Macro-F1 and raw SURE-RAG reaches 0.8951, substantially above DeBERTa mean-pooling at 0.6516 and comparable to the strong concat cross-encoder at 0.8888.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "VI-B Main HotpotQA-RAG v3 Results"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Set-level answer aggregation materially improves over pooling-only verification, supporting the paper's argument that evidence sufficiency cannot be reduced to selecting the individually most supportive passage.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "VI-H Ablation and VII-A Interpretation"
        },
        {
          "finding": "SURE-RAG provides a strong low-coverage selective-ranking benefit, but this advantage does not constitute a strict high-coverage or anytime-valid risk guarantee.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "VI-D Selective Answering and VII-A Interpretation"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Post-hoc calibration improves binary expected calibration error from 0.0304 to 0.0198 but does not improve Risk@30, which changes from 0.1642 to 0.1670.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "VI-E Calibration and Fixed-Risk Diagnostics"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Counterfactual swaps show near-perfect sensitivity to degradation of the evidence set on the controlled benchmark, including perfect reported success for partial, hard-insufficient, and irrelevant evidence substitutions.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "VI-F Counterfactual Evidence Swap"
        },
        {
          "finding": "External transfer exposes a sharp task boundary: SURE-RAG outperforms GPT-4o on the controlled HotpotQA-RAG v3 comparison, while GPT-4o strongly outperforms SURE-RAG for unsafe-answer detection on natural HaluBench.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "VI-G GPT-4o Judge and External Transfer"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Removing retrieval-uncertainty features reduces Macro-F1 from 0.8951 for raw SURE-RAG to 0.8370, indicating that the retrieval-information block is important in this constructed benchmark.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "VI-H Ablation"
        }
      ],
      "limitations": [
        "The principal benchmark is a controlled QA-derived construction rather than naturally occurring RAG logs or free-form long-form generation.",
        "The maximum shortcut-baseline artifact ratio is 0.6816, so the constructed benchmark retains moderate artifact risk.",
        "Entity-swap refutation generation can introduce answer-type mismatches and label noise.",
        "Experiments validate short-answer sufficiency rather than long-form multi-claim evidence completeness.",
        "The method targets controlled evidence sufficiency and does not generalize well to open-world hallucination detection in the reported HaluBench transfer.",
        "GPT-4o auditing supplements but does not replace large-scale human annotation.",
        "The aggregator combines local claim-passage signals rather than performing end-to-end reasoning jointly across passages.",
        "The selective score is empirically calibrated but does not furnish an anytime-valid or formal bounded-risk stopping guarantee.",
        "Temporal validity, evidence-version identity, permission-aware access, and adaptive decisions about what evidence to retrieve next are outside the evaluated method.",
        "The processed HotpotQA-RAG v3 files and evaluation artifacts are described as planned releases rather than already available artifacts in the paper."
      ],
      "reproducibility": {
        "code_available": false,
        "dataset_available": false,
        "metrics_reported": true
      },
      "confidence_scores": {
        "controlled_benchmark_macro_f1_gain": 0.99,
        "set_level_aggregation_advantage": 0.98,
        "low_coverage_selective_benefit": 0.98,
        "calibration_ece_but_not_risk_improvement": 0.99,
        "counterfactual_evidence_sensitivity": 0.99,
        "poor_natural_hallucination_transfer": 0.99,
        "retrieval_uncertainty_ablation_effect": 0.98
      },
      "raw_claims": [
        "SURE-RAG distinguishes supported, refuted, and insufficient evidence rather than treating retrieval relevance as sufficient grounding.",
        "A shared cross-encoder scores each claim-evidence pair before answer-level aggregation.",
        "The aggregator includes coverage, relation, uncertainty, and retrieval-derived feature blocks.",
        "The system abstains unless its predicted class is Supported and its uncertainty-adjusted score clears a development-selected threshold.",
        "HotpotQA-RAG v3 contains multiple evidence conditions derived from the same underlying questions and uses question-group-disjoint splits.",
        "Calibrated SURE-RAG has the highest reported Macro-F1 among the main controlled-benchmark configurations.",
        "Calibration lowers binary ECE but does not improve the reported Risk@30 value.",
        "The counterfactual evidence experiment shows that supported probability falls reliably when full evidence is replaced by degraded evidence.",
        "SURE-RAG transfers poorly to natural HaluBench unsafe-answer detection compared with GPT-4o.",
        "Pooling-only and the variant without retrieval uncertainty both perform materially below the full raw system.",
        "The authors characterize the current evidence as controlled-benchmark validation rather than a complete solution to open-world hallucination.",
        "Release of processed benchmark files, split identifiers, predictions, configurations, and evaluation scripts is described as planned."
      ],
      "source_url": "https://arxiv.org/html/2605.03534",

    }
